claims.text: Conventional preparation of single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering temperatures above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 has significant residual porosity.
Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 has inadequate mechanical strength for long-duration liquid-plating service.
Residual porosity and structural weakness in conventionally sintered ZrB2 lead to eventual component failure in liquid environments.
SPS is a substantially faster processing method than a prior conventional sintering route.
Computationally optimized SPS can fully densify single-phase ZrB2 at approximately 2000 °C.
SPS can reduce the ZrB2 preparation temperature from above 2300 °C to approximately 2000 °C.
Localized electric fields and applied pressure during SPS enhance atomic diffusion in ZrB2.
Enhanced diffusion during SPS promotes neck formation between ZrB2 particles.
SPS-induced diffusion and neck formation eliminate or substantially reduce intergranular pores.
Rapid pressure-assisted SPS accelerates ZrB2 densification at lower temperature than conventional sintering.
Computational optimization can select SPS parameters that avoid dwell times responsible for pore coarsening during conventional sintering.
Microstructural pores and defects provide pathways for liquid-plating-bath infiltration.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have a denser, nearly pore-free microstructure than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Reduced porosity in SPS-processed ZrB2 will improve its mechanical strength.
Reduced porosity in SPS-processed ZrB2 will improve resistance to liquid infiltration and degradation during 500–1000 hours of plating-bath exposure.
The degree of densification and mechanical-property improvement depends on the precise SPS heating rate, dwell time, and pressure.
Performance of the proposed optimized SPS conditions may not scale directly to larger or geometrically complex ZrB2 components.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires improved performance relative to the conventional control, but the falsification rule parenthetically treats 'comparable or better' performance as satisfying improvement. Comparable performance would not establish the predicted improvement.
